opus-5.5.text:
That's a really central question for us, and honestly, the answer is a lot more empirical than people expect. The tempting approach is to model everything as accurately as possible, but that's both very expensive and usually unnecessary. A high-fidelity simulation that runs a hundred times slower is often worse for training than a rough one you can run on thousands of robots in parallel.

So the way I think about it is: what does the policy actually need to be robust to? For legged locomotion, the things that really matter are the rigid-body dynamics of the robot itself, contacts with the ground, and especially the actuators. The actuator was the big lesson for us. The motors on a robot like ANYmal have their own dynamics. There are delays, the torque tracking isn't perfect, and there's friction in the gearboxes. If you treat the joints as ideal torque sources, the policy learns behaviors that look great in sim and just fall apart on hardware. We ended up learning an actuator model from real data, a small network that maps commands to actual torques, and that closed a huge part of the sim-to-real gap.

On the other hand, there are things we deliberately don't model precisely. Ground friction, the exact mass distribution, terrain compliance. Instead of trying to get those exactly right, we randomize them over a wide range. The policy then can't rely on any specific value and has to be robust across all of them. In a sense the real world just becomes one more sample from that distribution.

The process is usually iterative. You start simple, deploy on the real robot, watch where it fails, and figure out which missing physical effect explains the failure. If it's slipping, maybe your friction range is wrong. If it's oscillating, maybe you're missing latency in the observations. You add that, either by modeling it or randomizing it, and repeat. Over time you build up an understanding of which details are critical and which ones the policy can simply absorb through robustness.

And then there's the perception side, which is a different story. Rendering realistic camera images is hard, so we often avoid it entirely by using height maps or depth from simulated sensors and then adding noise and artifacts that mimic what the real sensors do. Again, you're not trying to be photorealistic. You're trying to make sure the policy sees the same kind of imperfections it will see on the real robot.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes modeling actuator dynamics and learning an actuator model from real data, but it never says the simulator must enforce the motors’ operating limits.

r002.rationale: It describes deploying on the real robot, observing failures, and using those observations to identify missing effects such as friction or latency; it also says the actuator model was learned from real data.

r003.rationale: The response favors simulation speed over modeling every detail generally, but says actuator dynamics are critical and does not state that speed takes priority over detailed actuator physics.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a bit of an art, honestly, and it's probably the question we spend the most time on. The naive answer would be "simulate everything as accurately as possible," but that's a trap. The more physical detail you add, the slower your simulation gets, and for the kind of massively parallel reinforcement learning we do, speed is the whole point. We're running thousands of robots in parallel on a single GPU, and that's what lets us train a locomotion policy in minutes instead of days. If I made the simulation ten times more accurate but ten times slower, I'd probably end up with a worse policy, because I'd have far fewer samples to learn from.

So the way I think about it is: what does the policy actually need to perceive and react to in order to do the task? For legged locomotion, the things that really matter are the contact dynamics, the rigid-body physics of the legs, the actuator behavior, and the terrain. Those have to be reasonably faithful. The contact model in particular is where a lot of the sim-to-real gap lives, because the moment a foot touches the ground is where simulators tend to be the most wrong.

Then there's a second category, which is things we don't try to model precisely but instead randomize over. Friction is a good example. I don't know the friction coefficient of the floor the robot will walk on, and I can't simulate it accurately anyway, so instead I sample it from a range during training and force the policy to be robust to it. Same with masses, motor strength, communication latency, small perturbations and pushes. The policy learns to handle a whole distribution of worlds rather than one specific world, and the real robot is hopefully just one more sample from that distribution.

And then there's a third category of things we deliberately leave out, because they're either too expensive or just not important for the behavior we care about. Deformable terrain, detailed thermal effects on the motors, that sort of thing. We don't model those at all unless we see a failure on the real robot that points directly at them.

That last part is really how the process works in practice. It's iterative. You train in sim, deploy on hardware, and watch what breaks. Very often the failure tells you exactly which physical detail is missing or which randomization range is too narrow. Early on, for instance, the actuators were a big one. The real motors on ANYmal have their own control loop, their own delays and saturation, and a pure torque-controlled rigid body simulation doesn't capture that. So the fix was to learn an actuator model from real data and plug that into the simulator. That's a detail you add because the robot told you to, not because you guessed it up front.

So the short version is: be faithful on the things the policy must sense and react to, randomize over the things you can't know, and skip the rest until reality proves you wrong.

r001.rationale: The response mentions motor delays and saturation and says to add an actuator model, but it does not state that the simulation must enforce the motors’ operating limits to prevent physically impossible behavior.

r002.rationale: It says real-hardware failures reveal missing physical details and describes learning an actuator model from real data, which communicates using real-robot measurements to identify simulator effects.

r003.rationale: It prioritizes simulation speed over fidelity in general, but also says actuator behavior must be reasonably faithful and describes adding an actuator model. It does not state that speed takes priority over detailed actuator physics.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to ask which physical details actually matter for the task. A simulation is always an approximation, so the goal isn’t to reproduce every detail of the real world. It’s to capture the things that affect the behavior you want the robot to learn.

For locomotion, for example, contact with the ground and the response of the actuators are very important. If the simulated motors react immediately, but the real motors have a delay, the policy can learn a behavior that works very well in simulation and fails on the robot. Adding detail somewhere else won’t necessarily fix that.

Then there are parameters you don’t know precisely, like friction or the mass of a component. You can vary those during training so the policy learns to handle a range of conditions instead of depending on one exact value. But you still need to test on the real system. You look at where the behavior differs, identify which assumptions might explain that difference, and improve the simulation where it matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses actuator response delays but does not say the simulation must enforce the real motors’ operating limits.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing on the real system and examining behavior differences, but does not state that real-robot measurements are used to identify which physical effects to simulate.

r003.rationale: The response does not prioritize simulation speed over detailed actuator physics; it instead says actuator response can be important to capture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to ask which details actually affect the behavior you want to learn. You don’t necessarily need a simulation that looks exactly like the real world. You need one that captures the interactions that matter for the task.

For a legged robot, for example, contact with the ground, friction, and the behavior of the actuators are very important. You can have a fairly simple visual model, but if the motors respond very differently in simulation than they do on the robot, the policy can learn something that won’t work in reality.

And then there are parameters that you don’t know precisely. Instead of trying to identify one perfect value for each of them, you can vary them during training—things like mass, friction, or delays—so the policy learns to work across a range of conditions. The important thing is to test on the real robot and use the failures to understand what your simulation is missing. It’s an iterative process.

r001.rationale: The response says actuator behavior should match the robot, but does not state that the simulator must enforce the motors’ operating limits or prevent physically impossible behavior.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing on the real robot and using failures to find what the simulation is missing, but does not describe using real-robot measurements to identify which physical effects to include.

r003.rationale: The response favors capturing task-relevant interactions and says a simple visual model can suffice, but does not say simulation speed takes priority over detailed actuator physics.
